title: Store water at home
summary: Store water in food-grade or clean soda bottles, sanitize them with bleach first, label them with the date, keep them cool and dark, and replace the water every 6 months.

list: Unopened, commercially bottled water is the safest and most reliable water in an emergency (CDC).
Keep it sealed in its original container in a cool, dark place (Ready.gov).
In normal times, replace it before its expiration date (CDC) or at least once a year (Red Cross), whichever comes first.
Once a bottle is open, use it. Don’t store it again (Red Cross).

blocks.p: Best: food-grade water storage containers (CDC, Ready.gov). Clean plastic soft drink bottles also work (FEMA, Red Cross).
If you can’t get food-grade containers, choose one that (CDC):

list: Has a top that closes tightly.
Is durable and unbreakable. Not glass.
Has a narrow neck or opening if possible, so you can pour from it.
Has no paper in the lid (Ohio State University Extension).

blocks.warn: Never use a container that held a toxic chemical, such as bleach, pesticides, other chemicals or oil. Tiny amounts can stay in the container (CDC, Washington State Department of Health, Ohio State University Extension).

list: Don’t use milk jugs or cartons: they don’t seal well and they break down (Red Cross).
Don’t use glass: it breaks (CDC, Red Cross).

blocks.p: Do this before you fill any container (CDC).

steps: Wash the container and cap with soap and water. Rinse until no soap is left.

Make the sanitizing solution: 1 teaspoon (5 mL) of plain, unscented liquid household chlorine bleach in 1 quart (4 cups, 0.95 L) of water. CDC gives this for bleach of 5% to 9% sodium hypochlorite, the usual strength in the US. Check the label.
Pour the solution into the container, cap it tightly and shake it well, so the solution touches every inside surface.
Wait at least 30 seconds, then pour the solution out.
Let the empty container air-dry before you fill it.

blocks.p: This solution is only for the empty container: pour it all out, and never drink it. To make drinking water safe, use the much smaller dose and the 30-minute wait in Make water safe.

blocks.warn: Never mix bleach with ammonia or any other cleaner (CDC). Indoors, open windows and doors, and try not to breathe the fumes.

steps: Water from a public supply treated with chlorine: fill straight from the tap, unless there is a boil-water notice. You don’t need to add anything (Ready.gov, Red Cross).

Water from a well or any supply not treated with chlorine: make it safe before you store it, as in Make water safe. Some water has contaminants that bleach cannot fix; if you have a private well, ask your health department in normal times how to store its water (Red Cross).
Fill the container to the top, unless it may freeze (see Freezing).
Cap it tightly. Don’t touch the inside of the cap with your fingers (Ready.gov).
Label it “Drinking water” with the date you filled it (CDC). A grease pencil or crayon on the lid works (University of Alaska Fairbanks Extension).

list: Somewhere cool: 50°F to 70°F (10°C to 21°C) (CDC).
Out of direct sunlight, in a dark place (CDC, Ready.gov).
Away from gasoline, pesticides and household cleaners (CDC, University of Alaska Fairbanks Extension).
Safe from flooding and freezing (Washington State Department of Health).
If you freeze water on purpose, leave 2 to 3 inches (5 to 8 cm) of air at the top so the container does not break as the water expands (Ohio State University Extension).
Use plastic: some glass breaks however much space you leave (Ohio State University Extension).
Jugs of water in a freezer that is not full help keep the food frozen longer when the power goes off (Ohio State University Extension).
Replace water you filled yourself every 6 months (CDC, Ready.gov, FEMA).
In an emergency, use bottled water for drinking, cooking and brushing teeth (CDC).
Keep water you have boiled or treated in clean, sanitized containers with tight covers (CDC).

sources.name: CDC, How to Create an Emergency Water Supply (reviewed June 27, 2025)
sources.used: Unopened commercially bottled water safest; expiration date; food-grade containers, or a tight top, durable unbreakable not glass, narrow neck; never containers that held toxic chemicals such as bleach or pesticides; wash with soap, rinse; 1 teaspoon unscented liquid household chlorine bleach in 1 quart (4 cups) of water, 5% to 9% sodium hypochlorite; cover, shake, touch all inside surfaces; wait at least 30 seconds, pour out; air-dry; label “drinking water” with the date; 50°F to 70°F; out of direct sunlight; away from gasoline or pesticides; replace every 6 months; use bottled water for drinking, cooking, brushing teeth

sources.name: CDC, How to Safely Clean and Sanitize with Bleach (reviewed August 26, 2026)
sources.used: Never mix bleach with ammonia or any other cleaner; open windows and doors indoors, try not to breathe fumes; 5% to 9% is the most common concentration in the US

sources.name: CDC, How to Make Water Safe in an Emergency (reviewed September 19, 2024)
sources.used: Store boiled or treated water in clean, sanitized containers with tight covers

sources.name: Ready.gov (FEMA), Water; Ready.gov, Storing Water in Plastic Soda Bottles (last updated 09/18/2011)
sources.used: Commercially bottled water sealed in its original container in a cool, dark place; food-grade containers; chlorinated utility tap water needs nothing added; well or unchlorinated water needs bleach; fill to the top; cap tightly without touching the inside of the cap; date the container; replace home-filled water every six months

sources.name: FEMA, American Red Cross and USDA, Food and Water in an Emergency
sources.used: Plastic containers such as soft drink bottles are best; never a container that held toxic substances; seal, label, store in a cool, dark place; rotate every six months

sources.name: American Red Cross, Disaster Supplies Kit (University of Missouri Extension EMW1012, reviewed July 2025)
sources.used: Food-grade containers with tight lids; milk containers do not seal well; avoid milk cartons and glass bottles; utility-treated water need not be treated before storing; some sources have contaminants bleach cannot neutralize, and only the local public health agency should advise on storing and treating them; keep bottled water sealed, replace at least once a year, once opened use it and do not store it

sources.name: National Disaster Education Coalition (American Red Cross, FEMA and others), Talking About Disaster: Disaster Supplies Kit
sources.used: Avoid containers that will decompose or break, such as milk cartons or glass bottles; soft drink bottles; replace every six months

sources.name: Washington State Department of Health, Treating Drinking Water for Emergency Use (DOH 331-115, July 2022)
sources.used: Never reuse a container that held pesticides, chemicals or oil; seal and label with the date; store safe from flooding and freezing

sources.name: Ohio State University Extension, Preserving Water for Emergency Use (HYG-5354, 2017)
sources.used: Never a container that held toxic substances, tiny amounts remain; lids without paper; leave 2 to 3 inches of air space before freezing; plastic preferred, some glass breaks; frozen water helps keep food frozen in an outage

sources.name: University of Alaska Fairbanks Cooperative Extension, Emergency Water Supply (SAL-00006, 2021)
sources.used: Mark the fill date on the lid with a red crayon or grease pencil; store away from household cleaners

sources.name: FDA, Guidelines for Determining Metric Equivalents of Household Measures; USGS, Facts About Water
sources.used: 1 teaspoon means 5 mL (FDA); 1 gallon = 4 quarts = 3.7854 liters, so 1 quart is 0.95 L (USGS)
